key_insight: Large language models can often learn improved reasoning from weaker reward signals, but success depends strongly on model scale, domain complexity, and the mix of clean vs noisy supervision.
problem_solved: Determines when reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains effective under weak supervision (scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervision), providing practical guidance for deploying RL-based reasoning improvements when high-quality reward labels are hard to obtain.
method: Systematic empirical study across multiple model families and reasoning domains to evaluate RLVR under three weak-supervision regimes: scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervision.
Controlled experiments that vary model scale, reward noise level, and amount of verified data to identify factors that enable or block learning.
Analysis of success conditions and mitigation strategies (e.g., mixing small verified reward sets with noisy/self-supervised signals, reward calibration, and curriculum-style training).
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners actionable rules-of-thumb for when to invest in costly reward annotation versus relying on weaker signals, and suggests practical training strategies to extend RLVR benefits to larger models and realistic low-label settings.
visual_elements: Flowchart of experimental setup: model families → three weak-supervision regimes → evaluation metrics
Heatmap or matrix showing success likelihood as a function of model scale (rows) and reward quality/data quantity (columns)
Bar chart comparing performance gains across the three supervision types with and without small amounts of verified rewards
Icons/illustrations for the three weak supervision modes (scarce data, noisy rewards, self-supervision) and a checklist of practical recommendations
paper_title: When Can LLMs Learn to Reason with Weak Supervision?
paper_authors: Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, Anna Mordvina, Hamid Palangi, Saadia Gabriel
